newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl says euro must be strong, EMU criteria strict.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says euro must be strong, EMU criteria strict.

text.p: German chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Wednesday it was essential that the future European currency be strong and that he would fight any attempt to weaken the entry criteria in the Maastricht Treaty.
In an article written for the Boersen-Zeitung newspaper, Kohl said "The giving up of the mark and the launch of the euro is the most difficult European question for us Germans.
"For that reason I will continue to combat energetically any moves which go in the direction of softening the Mastricht criteria," he added.

Germany has consistently taken a tough line on entry criteria for European monetary union even though it shows increasing signs of itself failing to reach the targets on public budgets and debt in their strictest definitions.

A survey of 32 economists conducted by Reuters showed that five of the six countries expected to form the launch pad for a single currency were well on their way to meeting the required criteria for entry, but that Germany may lag behind.

Germany is seen overshooting slightly on the goal that its 1997 budget deficit fall to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP)and its debt to 60 percent of GDP, with a predicted deficit ratio of 3.05 percent and debt-to-GDP of 62 percent.
In the article, Kohl noted that Germany still had a lot of work to do to meet the entry goals.
But he added that all German government authorities -- at federal, state and local levels -- were determined to reach the goal so as to create the basis for a solid euro.
"Our aim is to have as many EU member states in European economic and monetary union at the start in 1999 so that it gains economic weight from the start," Kohl said.
